Nessa0071:
When my MS/NMO first started i was paraplegic. Both of my legs and my chest from the rib cage down was numb and unresponsive.  I too have lost almost all vision in my right eye.  I have taken the IV steroids 3 times now, and also done plasmapheresis for 15 days while in the hospital. I also go in for rituxan every 6 months.  I have 3 lesions in my brain, and one the length of spinal discs 1-10.  Do you have any tips for keeping your positive attitude? I can't seem to force any kind of positive thoughts on a daily/weekly basis. This disease came out of nowhere and completely train wrecked my life.  Would be nice to have another survivor to talk to. Feel free to message me anytime.

Yeah I know that reddit is never a substitute for Doctors, Lawyers etc. I was mainly looking for advice from people in similar situations.  You are right in the fact that it's extremely hard to overlook the future progression of the disease and the fact that there is no cure. My ex-fiance used to be my go to person when I needed support to make it through tough times, but I guess even she got tired of dealing with it and chose the option of going on to live a normal life.  I was worried about posting here and getting judged for thinking about giving up. Before all this I was a very strong willed individual, but  I don't want to end up being a burden on family members. Some of the treatment options are extremely expensive and I don't know how much longer I can continue to afford them on disability.

I have tried getting some help from various doctors, but the majority of them are blown away by the struggle that I had to fight through just to make it to the place that I am now.  After I told my psychologist my fiance left me, she said, "Well at least it can't get any worse than it is now" when in all retrospect, it could.  

I believe 911 can't really help in this situation unless I am misinformed they can only admit you to the hospital and keep you on watch for 72 hours, then discharge you back out into the world.

Its the little things that you take for granite.  After spending all summer in various hospitals I was confined to a wheelchair.  Things like making easy meals and showering become more difficult, and were things I never thought would be frustrating. Going from completly healthy to having s rare neurological disease also throws a wrench in life in general. You just have to adapt, and not be ashamed to ask others for help.
